rows.text: # Industrial production of antibiotics, alcoholic beverages, citric acid ## 1. Introduction Opening frame for **Industrial production of antibiotics** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Microbes in Human Welfare fill pass. ## 2.…  ·  The same fermentation principle, scaled to tonnes: a **fermenter** (bioreactor) grows the microbe under controlled temperature, pH and aeration, and the product is harvested, purified and marketed. The three NEB exemplars: **penicillin** (the first antibiotic, discovered by Fleming in 1928, mass-produced in WWII), **ethanol** for beverages (*Saccharomyces*), and **citric acid** (*Aspergillus niger*).

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: Antibiotic: Penicillium notatum/chrysogenum → penicillin (Fleming 1928, Chain & Florey purified); 'antibiotic' = against life — the discovery story earns the mark.  ·  Trick 2: Alcohol: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (brewer's yeast) ferments malted grains/fruit juice; distilled spirits vs beer/wine — the yeast is the same in all.

rows.text: **Most-asked points (NEB).** (1) Name the microbe for penicillin, ethanol and citric acid. (2) Draw and label a fermenter. (3) Why must the fermenter be aerated for penicillin but not for ethanol? (4) List the stages from discovery to market. (5) What is downstream processing?  ·  ## 8. Summary and self-check 5–10 line chapter summary, self-check questions and the common-confusions list (block VIII) — completed in the unit fill pass.  ·  **Summary.** Industrial fermentation = strain + medium + controlled bioreactor + downstream processing. Penicillin (fungus, aerobic), ethanol (yeast, anaerobic) and citric acid (fungus, aerobic) are the three exemplars. **Self-check:** can you label six parts of a fermenter and state each one's job?
